mcqs.question: What's the key distinction that makes an LLM-based system an "agent" rather than a single LLM call answering a question?
options: The model repeatedly decides what action to take next, that action has a real effect, and the result feeds back in for another decision — a loop, not a single response
Agents always use a larger, more capable model than single-call systems
Agents never produce a final text answer, only tool calls
Agents require a multi-agent setup with more than one model involved
mcqs.explanation: The defining feature is the loop: deciding an action, executing it, observing the result, and deciding again, as many times as needed — not the model size, and not that it can only call tools with no final text answer. A single agent (one model in a loop) is still an agent; multiple agents are a separate, optional pattern.

mcqs.question: Who actually executes a tool call requested by an LLM agent?
options: The LLM itself executes the action directly inside its own runtime
The surrounding application code executes the requested action, then feeds the result back into the model's context
The tool call is executed by a separate LLM dedicated only to running tools
Tool calls are never actually executed; they're purely illustrative text
mcqs.explanation: The model only ever emits a structured request naming a tool and arguments — it has no ability to execute anything itself. The application runs the real action and returns the result as the next observation, which is also exactly why sandboxing and permission checks belong in the application layer, not the model.

mcqs.question: What's the main trade-off between single-shot planning and iterative replanning in an agent?
options: Single-shot planning is always slower because it requires more LLM calls
Iterative replanning cannot use tools, only single-shot planning can

Single-shot planning is faster and more predictable but brittle if an early step's result invalidates later steps; iterative replanning is more robust to surprises but costs more calls and is less predictable upfront
There is no meaningful difference; both produce identical behavior
mcqs.explanation: Single-shot plans commit upfront, which is cheap and predictable but fragile if reality diverges from the plan; iterative replanning adapts step by step at the cost of more calls and less predictable total cost. Tool use is compatible with either approach, and the two approaches genuinely differ in robustness and cost profile.

mcqs.question: Why is a hard external step/cost limit considered a required safety rail for agents, rather than an optional tuning parameter?
options: Because the model's own confidence score reliably signals when to stop
Because LLM APIs automatically stop agent loops after a fixed number of calls with no configuration needed
Because agents are only vulnerable to infinite loops when using open-source models
Because nothing structurally guarantees the model will recognize it's stuck or done — it can loop indefinitely, burning real cost, without an external cap forcing a stop
mcqs.explanation: There's no built-in mechanism ensuring an agent self-terminates correctly; a model can misjudge progress or get stuck retrying, so an external hard limit is the only reliable backstop. APIs don't auto-cap agent loops for you, the model type doesn't determine this risk, and models don't have a reliable built-in stopping confidence signal.

mcqs.question: A task's steps can be fully enumerated in advance and never branch based on intermediate results. What's the most appropriate architecture?
options: A fixed prompt chain, since it's simpler, more predictable, and easier to debug when the steps are already known
A full autonomous agent, since agents are always the more capable and reliable choice
A multi-agent system with at least three specialized agents
Neither — this task cannot be solved with an LLM at all
mcqs.explanation: When steps are known upfront and don't need to adapt to intermediate results, a fixed chain gets the predictability and simplicity benefit without paying for an agent's dynamic decision-making overhead. A full agent or multi-agent system adds complexity this task doesn't need, and the task is clearly solvable with an LLM.
